catalog_quote: There are two additional symbols. The colon (:) marks long vowels, which contrast phonemically with short vowels. The stress mark (–) is used to mark words in which stress does not fall on the penultimate syllable. ... The vowels combine with each other in the following vowel sequences: ie, ia, iu, ei, ea, eu, ai, ae, au, ui, ue, ua, oi, oe, oa, and ou. These sequences do not constitute diphthongs, of which there are none in Asilulu. Consequently, when such a sequence occurs at the end of a word, unless otherwised marked, stress always falls on the penultimate syllable, that is the first vowel of the sequence. Similarly, when long vowels (i:, e:, a:, u:, o:) appear at the end of a word, stress falls on that vowel. [p. xxvii] ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the (root) word by default; every vowel counts as a syllable (there are no diphthongs), so a word-final vowel sequence is stressed on its first vowel, and a word-final long vowel is stressed (Collins treats V: as equivalent to VV, fn 29). Words whose stress is not penultimate are lexically marked with an acute accent in the dictionary (e.g. harám 'forbidden', an Arabic loan, p. 18). Pronominal clitics attached to a word do not move its stress (p. xxviii: 'the addition of clitic pronominal markers does not affect the original stress of the cliticized word'; [ratakeru] keeps the stress of ratak), which is also the point of Collins 1983 p. 82: Asilulu stress stays on the penult of the root under suffixation, unlike the Hoamoal languages where it shifts.
new_statements.exceptions: Words with non-penultimate stress exist and are marked with the stress mark in the dictionary; the marked headwords seen are loanwords with final stress (harám, from Arabic). Word-final long vowels take the stress. Cliticized/suffixed words keep root stress, so surface stress can be antepenultimate or earlier in such forms (Collins 1983 p. 82: húlane, ʔúlule, ráwaʔe, palaʔékni).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (dictionary headwords, citation forms); the clitic remark concerns host+pronominal-clitic words. No phrase-level or instrumental data.
new_statements.identity_note: Collins 2003 describes the Asilulu of Asilulu village proper (Nuclear Asilulu); he notes three dialects (Asilulu, Ureng, Hena Lima/Negeri Lima) and that the fricative r is a village-level marker. No separate dialect glottocodes involved; the statement is for asil1242 as a whole.

new_statements.quote: Omtrent den klemtoon is op te merken, dat deze, evenals zulks in 't Maleisch veelvuldig het geval is, in den regel valt op de voorlaatste lettergreep. In de dialecten van Harœkœ en Asilœlœ evenwel verspringt de klemtoon meermalen, en dikwijls op zeer grillige wijze. — Waar dit het geval is zal het teeken (') boven de lettergreep aanduiden, dat daarop de klemtoon vallen moet. — Nog zij aangeteekend, dat de vocaal in de lettergreep, waarop de klemtoon valt, in den regel lang moet worden uitgesproken.
new_statements.translation: Regarding the stress it is to be noted that, as is very often the case in Malay, it as a rule falls on the penultimate syllable. In the dialects of Haruku and Asilulu, however, the stress shifts many times, and often in a very capricious manner. — Where this is the case the sign (') above the syllable will indicate that the stress must fall on it. — It should further be noted that the vowel of the syllable on which the stress falls must as a rule be pronounced long.
new_statements.citation: van Hoëvell, G. W. W. C. 1877. Iets over de voornaamste dialecten der Ambonsche landtaal (bahasa tanah). Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 25: 1-136.
new_statements.locator: Section 'KLANKSTELSEL, KLEMTOON en UITSPRAAK', pp. 13-14 (PDF pp. 85-86 of the archive.org volume scan); dialect characterisation p. 11 (PDF p. 83); stress-marked examples p. 12 (PDF p. 84). Quote verified against the page images.
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's penultimate default (and with Collins 2003's use of a stress mark only for non-penultimate words), but adds that Asilulu is one of the two dialects where non-penultimate stress is frequent; his marked Asilulu examples are consistent with Collins 1983 p. 82 (stress on the penult of the root, suffixes do not shift it), which turns his 'capricious' shifts into a regular root-domain rule for at least the -ne citation forms. He also adds that the stressed vowel is as a rule long (cf. Collins 2003 on contrastive length).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Across the Ambon land-language dialects stress falls as a rule on the penultimate syllable (as in Malay); the stressed vowel is as a rule long. Van Hoëvell singles out the Haruku and Asilulu dialects as those in which the stress frequently departs from the penult 'in a very capricious manner', and marks such words with an acute in his wordlist. His own marked Asilulu examples on p. 12 (hœ́reader 'moon', laláhane 'companion', námane 'roadstead', beside Saparua hœlánno, lahánno) show the stress sitting on the penult of the root with the citation suffix -ne outside the stress domain, i.e. antepenultimate on the surface.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 11: '’t Verschil bestaat evenwel alleen in ’t leggen van den klemtoon. Terwijl de christen-inlander op Harœkœ den algemeenen regel volgt om ’t accent te leggen op de voorlaatste lettergreep, laat de Mohamedaan den klemtoon gedurig verspringen.' (On Haruku the Christian villages follow the general penultimate rule while the Muslim villages Pelauw, Kailolo, Kabauw, Rohomoni let the stress shift constantly.) p. 12: -ne forms of the Asilulu and Hila dialects carry 'gewijzigden klemtoon' (modified stress) relative to the -no/-nno forms of Haruku and Saparua. Also (p. 8, general remark) dialect differences arise partly 'door verschil in ’t leggen van den klemtoon' whereby long vowels become short and vice versa.
new_statements.identity_note: Van Hoëvell 1877 describes the 'negori ampat' dialect spoken west of Hila in Seit, Lima, Oering (Ureng) and Asilœlœ (his œ = /u/, i.e. Asiloeloe = Asilulu); in the wordlist '(Asil:) beteekent Asilœlœ' (p. 11), so the statements are about the Asilulu village dialect itself, alongside the Hila, Haruku (Pelauw), Saparua and Nusalaut dialects. The stress passage names 'Asilœlœ' explicitly.

readall_conflicts: Mild tension in characterisation, not in placement. Van Hoëvell 1877 (pp. 13-14) gives penultimate as the general rule for the Ambon land-language but says that in the Asilulu (and Haruku) dialect the stress 'shifts many times, and often in a very capricious manner', which reads as a heavier exception load than Collins 2003's introduction (stress mark used only for the words whose stress is not penultimate) or Collins 1983 p. 82 (stress on the penult of the root, unaffected by suffixes). His own marked Asilulu forms on p. 12 (hœ́reader, laláhane, námane, all root-penult + -ne) fit Collins 1983's root-domain rule exactly, so the 'capricious' shifts are at least partly the citation-suffix effect that Collins later regularised; the remaining lexically marked cases (e.g. Collins 2003 harám from Arabic) are exceptions to a penultimate default in every source. No source places Asilulu stress anywhere other than the penult by default.

sources.note: p. 82 (PDF p. 92): 'An important phonological rule distinguishes all Hoamoal languages from Asilulu. Stress in Hoamoal languages is always penultimate; if a suffix or particle is added to the word the stress shifts accordingly. In Asilulu this is not the case. The stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root word; additions of suffixes do not affect this stress.' Examples Asilulu húlane 'moon', ʔúlule 'kind of fruit', ráwaʔe 'tomorrow' vs Luhu hulané etc; Asilulu palaʔékni 'recall him'.
